title: Selected work
allDescription: Case studies from client work and my own products: storefronts, data tools, design systems and developer tooling.

projects.title: Aurora Commerce
projects.description: A headless storefront with fluid page transitions and a sub-second checkout flow.

image.alt: Abstract fluid gradient in warm and cool tones

blocks.lead: Aurora is the online flagship for an independent fashion label. They wanted the storefront to feel like their printed lookbooks, without giving up the speed and conversion of a conventional Shopify theme.

blocks.label: The problem
blocks.heading: A beautiful theme that nobody could buy from
body: The previous store was a heavily customised Liquid theme. Every campaign added another slider, another font and another tracking script, and by the time we started the median mobile page took 6.8 seconds to become interactive.

Editors also had no way to tell a story: product pages were templates, and campaign pages were static images exported from Figma. The brief was to keep Shopify as the source of truth for products and checkout, and rebuild everything the customer sees.

images.alt: Clothing store interior with garments on rails and shelves
Neutral-toned garments hanging on a minimal rail

blocks.caption: Campaign photography drives the layout: product grids adapt to the art direction of each collection.

items.title: Statically rendered, revalidated on demand
items.body: Every product and collection page is pre-rendered at build time. Shopify webhooks revalidate only the pages affected by a change, so prices and stock are fresh within seconds without rebuilding the site.

items.title: Editorial blocks instead of templates
items.body: Campaign pages are composed from a small set of blocks in the CMS: full-bleed images, product rails and long-form text. Editors arrange them freely; each block is responsible for its own loading and motion.

items.title: Transitions that respect the network
items.body: Shared-element transitions connect the grid to the product page, but the next page is prefetched on intent and the animation never waits on data. On slow connections it degrades to a plain crossfade.

blocks.label: Under the hood
blocks.caption: Shopify webhooks invalidate only the cache tags of the product or collection that changed.

blocks.alt: Shopping app open on a phone held above a laptop
blocks.caption: Over 70% of orders come from mobile, so every interaction was designed for the thumb first.

blocks.quote: For the first time, our website looks like the brand we photograph. And it sells more than the old one ever did.
blocks.author: Inês Moreira

projects.title: Pulse Analytics
projects.description: A real-time analytics dashboard rendering millions of data points at 60fps.

image.alt: Analytics dashboard with charts on a laptop screen

blocks.lead: Pulse gives the operations team of a European logistics company a live view of more than 12,000 vehicles, and lets them dig into years of route history without waiting on a report.

blocks.alt: Aerial view of a container port with cranes and stacked containers

blocks.label: Context
blocks.heading: Charts that fell over at fleet scale
body: The existing dashboard drew every vehicle and route as SVG. It worked for a regional depot, but with the whole fleet loaded the browser spent more time on layout than on drawing, and filtering a week of data froze the tab for several seconds.
Dispatchers had stopped using it. They exported CSVs into spreadsheets instead, which meant decisions were made on data that was already hours old.

items.label: CSV exports in the last quarter

blocks.label: Architecture
blocks.heading: From the GPU down to the database

items.title: Instanced rendering
items.body: Vehicles and route segments are drawn as instanced geometry in a single draw call per layer. Positions live in typed arrays and only the ranges that changed are uploaded each frame.

items.title: Filtering on the GPU
items.body: Time-range and status filters are uniforms, not array operations. Brushing across a month of history changes two numbers and the shader discards what falls outside, so interaction stays smooth on mid-range laptops.

items.title: Pre-aggregated history
items.body: A Go service rolls raw telemetry into ClickHouse materialised views at several resolutions. Zooming out asks for coarser buckets, so the client never receives more points than it can show.

blocks.caption: Partial buffer updates keep the per-frame upload under 200 KB, even with the whole fleet moving.

images.alt: Warehouse with long rows of shelving and stacked yellow crates
Truck driving on an open road under a blue sky

blocks.caption: Depots and drivers on the same timeline: a delay at a warehouse shows up on every route it affects.

blocks.label: Learnings
blocks.heading: Performance is a product feature
body: The biggest change wasn't technical. Once filtering became instant, dispatchers started asking questions they had never bothered to ask, and the tool became the place where planning happens.
We now treat interaction latency like any other requirement, with budgets per view that are checked on every pull request.

projects.title: Lumen Studio
projects.description: An immersive portfolio for an architecture studio, driven by custom shaders.

blocks.lead: An immersive portfolio for an architecture studio that designs with natural light. The site had to feel like walking through one of their buildings, and still load fast on a phone at a construction site.

images.alt: White angular building facade against a pale sky
Curved orange architectural walls against a blue sky

blocks.quote: We don't design buildings, we design how light moves through them. The website finally shows that.
blocks.author: Tomás Valente

blocks.label: Concept
blocks.heading: Every project as a light study
body: Instead of a grid of thumbnails, each project opens as a single image that a shader relights as you scroll. Light enters from one side, crosses the facade and fades out, mirroring a day in the building in a few seconds of scrolling.
Typography sits on top of the image and reacts to the same light, so text casts soft shadows that move with the sun.

blocks.alt: Undulating white facade curving against a clear blue sky
blocks.caption: The light pass is computed per pixel, so the same shader works on every photograph without manual masks.

blocks.label: The shader

blocks.alt: Bright living room interior with large windows and wood panelling
blocks.caption: Interiors use a softer, indirect light pass so rooms read as calm rather than dramatic.

projects.title: Terminal Notes
projects.description: A keyboard-first note taking app for developers, with local-first sync.

image.alt: Code displayed on a dark monitor

blocks.lead: Terminal Notes is a keyboard-first note taking app for developers. It started as a weekend project to replace a folder of Markdown files and now has a few thousand daily users.

blocks.label: Why
blocks.heading: Notes that live where I work
body: I kept losing snippets, commands and half-finished thoughts across editors, chats and sticky notes. Existing apps were either built for writers, with lots of formatting and little speed, or synced through a server I didn't control.
The goal was simple: open, type, close, all without touching the mouse, with everything stored locally and syncing between my machines when they're online.

blocks.alt: Person working at a desk with several bright monitors in a dark room

items.title: Command palette for everything
items.body: Every action, from creating a note to moving it between workspaces, is a fuzzy-searchable command. Shortcuts are learned by using the palette, which shows the key binding next to each result.

items.title: Local-first by default
items.body: Notes are stored in SQLite on disk and work completely offline. There's no account to create; sync is opt-in and peer to peer.

items.title: Conflict-free sync
items.body: Each note is a CRDT document. Edits made on two machines while offline merge automatically when they reconnect, with no 'which version do you want to keep' dialogs.

blocks.label: Sync
blocks.caption: Merging is the CRDT's job; the app only decides when to persist.

images.alt: Python source code on a dark editor theme
HTML and SVG markup with colourful syntax highlighting

blocks.caption: Code blocks are highlighted with the same grammars as VS Code, so snippets look the way they do in your editor.

blocks.quote: It's the first notes app I haven't fought with. It's just there when I hit the shortcut.
blocks.author: Priya Raman

blocks.label: Next
blocks.heading: What's coming
body: The next release adds a CLI, so notes can be created and searched straight from the terminal, and shared workspaces for small teams that still don't require a server.

projects.title: Relay
projects.description: A design system that gave a digital bank one visual language across web, iOS and Android.

image.alt: Stylus on a tablet next to a backlit keyboard in a dark room

blocks.lead: Relay is the design system behind a fast-growing digital bank. Eleven product teams were shipping the same buttons, forms and charts in slightly different ways; Relay replaced them with one set of tokens and components that every platform builds from.

images.alt: Hand sketching wireframes of screens on paper
Interface sketches drawn on a tablet next to a keyboard

blocks.caption: Everything started on paper: an audit of 140 screens grouped into the patterns they actually shared.

blocks.quote: Relay turned design reviews from arguing about pixels into talking about the customer.
blocks.author: Marta Sousa

blocks.label: Concept
blocks.heading: Decisions, not components
body: The audit found 23 shades of 'primary blue' and nine button heights. The problem wasn't missing components, it was that nobody had written down the decisions behind them.

So Relay starts with tokens: colour, type, spacing and motion as named decisions in a single source. Components are built on those tokens, which means changing a decision updates every platform at once.

blocks.alt: Product team working together on laptops around a shared table
blocks.caption: Each product team has a Relay champion who reviews new patterns before they reach the core library.

blocks.label: Tokens

blocks.alt: Speaker presenting to colleagues in a bright open office
blocks.caption: Monthly Relay sessions walk teams through new tokens and components before they ship.

projects.title: Harbor
projects.description: An open-source deployment tool that ships Docker apps to your own servers with one command.

image.alt: Laptop partly open in the dark, its screen glowing in red and blue

blocks.lead: Harbor deploys Docker applications to servers you own, with zero-downtime rollouts and automatic HTTPS, from a single command. It's what I wanted after years of choosing between expensive platforms and hand-written deploy scripts.

blocks.label: Why
blocks.heading: Platforms are great until the bill arrives
body: Hosted platforms make deploying feel effortless, but their pricing grows with every side project, and a single VPS can run a dozen small apps for a fraction of the cost.
The catch is everything a platform does for you: building images, swapping containers without downtime, certificates, rollbacks. Harbor does those parts and nothing else.

blocks.alt: Server rack with neatly bundled network cables

items.title: Zero-downtime rollouts
items.body: New containers start next to the old ones and receive traffic only after their health check passes. If it fails, the old version keeps serving and the deploy is marked failed.

items.title: HTTPS by default
items.body: Harbor configures Caddy as the edge proxy, so every app gets a certificate from Let's Encrypt the first time it's deployed, with renewals handled automatically.

items.title: Rollbacks in seconds
items.body: Every release is kept as a tagged image. `harbor rollback` points traffic back to the previous one without rebuilding anything.

blocks.label: Config
blocks.code:
app = "invoice-api"
image = "ghcr.io/acme/invoice-api"

[servers]
web = ["10.0.0.12", "10.0.0.13"]

[proxy]
host = "api.example.com"
healthcheck = "/healthz"

[env]
clear = { PORT = "8080" }
secret = ["DATABASE_URL", "STRIPE_KEY"]
blocks.caption: A complete configuration: `harbor deploy` reads this, builds, pushes and rolls out to both servers.

images.alt: Network switch with blue and grey ethernet cables plugged in
Code on a laptop screen lit by blue and purple light

blocks.caption: Harbor talks to servers over plain SSH; there's no agent to install and nothing listening on extra ports.

blocks.quote: We moved nine services off our PaaS in an afternoon. The bill went from four figures to a coffee a day.
blocks.author: Daniel Okafor

blocks.label: Next
blocks.heading: What's coming
body: Version 2 adds built-in database backups to object storage and a small web dashboard for teams who'd rather not live in the terminal.
